chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Is'haq ibn Abd al-Aziz, from one of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

We are on the road to Mecca and wish to enter the state of Ihram, so we apply oil, but there is no lime with us with which we scrub off the oil, so we scrub with flour. And a thought entered me regarding that, which Allah knows best. He said: 'Is it fear of extravagance?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'There is no extravagance in what improves the body. Indeed, I sometimes order the pure [oil] to be rubbed in with oil, so I massage with it. But rather, extravagance is in what spoils wealth and harms the body.'

I said: 'So what is austerity?' He said: 'Eating bread and salt while you are able to have something else.' I said: 'So what is moderation?' He said: 'Bread, meat, milk, vinegar, and butter; once this and once that.'

key_terms.إِحْرَامٌ: State of consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.النُّورَةُ: Lime paste used for hair removal

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic definition of extravagance and moderation in personal care and diet according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) refutes the common misconception that using high-quality oil for body care during Ihram constitutes extravagance, defining true israf as waste that harms wealth or the body rather than the quality of the substance. He further distinguishes moderation (qasd) from both excess and undue austerity, prescribing a balanced diet of bread, meat, milk, vinegar, and butter as the ideal standard for the believer. This hadith is foundational in Shia jurisprudence for understanding the permissibility of using premium goods in worship when done with gratitude and without waste.
